questions.q: A trader in Latur buys 132 kg of jowar from one farm and 156 kg from another. She packs it in bags of equal whole-kg weight, each bag holding grain from one farm only, and wants as few bags as possible. Which plan does she choose?
questions.a: 24 bags of 12 kg each: the common factors of 132 and 156 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, the highest is 12, and 132/12 + 156/12 = 11 + 13 = 24 bags.

questions.q: In the jump game, Jumpy starts at 0 and uses one jump size throughout. For one pair of treasure positions, the longest jump size that lands on both treasures is exactly 6. Which pair is it?
questions.a: 42 and 66: their common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, so the longest jump is 6. For 36 and 60 a jump of 6 lands on both, but 12 is longer; 6 does not land on 45, and 24 and 40 have longest jump 8.

questions.q: Rice from two farms weighs 72 kg and 120 kg and is to be packed in bags of equal whole-kg weight, one farm per bag, using as few bags as possible. Mohan writes: 'The common factors of 72 and 120 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 and 24, so each bag holds 24 kg and 8 bags are needed.' Check each part of his working and say how far he is right.
questions.a: Partly right. His list misses 8: 72 = 8 x 9 and 120 = 8 x 15, so the common factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. The highest is still 24, so his bag weight of 24 kg is right, and 72/24 + 120/24 = 3 + 5 = 8 bags is also right. The missing factor did not change the answer only because it was smaller than 24.
s: finds that 8 is missing from the list of common factors
confirms the HCF 24 kg is still correct
confirms 3 + 5 = 8 bags and gives the verdict partly right

questions.q: A school gardener fills a 60-litre tank and an 84-litre tank using one bucket of whole-litre capacity. Each tank must be filled exactly with full buckets. (a) By listing factors, find every bucket size that works for both tanks. (b) Which bucket needs the fewest fills in all, and how many fills is that? (c) The store only has buckets of 10 litres or less. Which bucket should he take now, and how many fills does it need in all?
questions.a: (a) Factors of 60: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60; factors of 84: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 12, 14, 21, 28, 42, 84. Common factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. (b) The biggest, 12 litres (the HCF): 60/12 + 84/12 = 5 + 7 = 12 fills. (c) The largest common factor that is at most 10 is 6 litres (10 is not a factor of 84): 10 + 14 = 24 fills.
s: (a) common factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 found by listing
(b) 12-litre bucket (the HCF) and 12 fills
(c) 6-litre bucket chosen because 10 does not divide 84, and 24 fills

questions.q: True or False: For a room 35 ft by 56 ft, square tiles of side 7 ft are the largest whole-foot tiles that fit the floor exactly, and 40 such tiles are needed. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The factors of 35 are 1, 5, 7, 35 and of 56 are 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 14, 28, 56, so the common factors are 1 and 7 and the HCF is 7 ft. The floor takes 35/7 = 5 tiles along one side and 56/7 = 8 along the other, so 5 x 8 = 40 tiles.
s: verdict True
reason: common factors 1 and 7 give HCF 7, and 5 x 8 = 40 tiles

questions.q: Meena says she has found two numbers whose common factors are exactly 1, 2, 4 and 6, nothing else. (a) Show that her list cannot be complete. (b) Check your reasoning on the numbers 24 and 36 by listing their common factors.
questions.a: (a) 6 is a common factor, so each number is 6 times something. Since 3 is a factor of 6, 3 is also a factor of each number. So 3 must be a common factor, and a list without 3 is impossible. (b) Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24; factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Both 4 and 6 appear, and so does 3 (and also 12).
s: (a) since 6 divides both numbers and 3 divides 6, 3 divides both
(a) concludes the list without 3 is impossible
(b) common factors of 24 and 36 listed as 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, showing 3 appears

questions.q: A dairy in Anand has 150 litres of milk and 225 litres of buttermilk. Each is poured into cans of the same whole-litre size, one drink per can, with nothing left over. (a) List the factors of 150 and of 225, and their common factors. (b) What can size gives the fewest cans, and how many cans is that? (c) The supplier stocks only 15 L, 25 L, 30 L and 50 L cans. Which of these sizes can be used? Give a reason for each one you reject. (d) A 15 L can costs Rs 20 and a 25 L can costs Rs 35. Which of the two usable sizes is cheaper overall? Show the cost of each and say whether the fewest cans is also the cheapest choice.
questions.a: (a) Factors of 150: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 25, 30, 50, 75, 150. Factors of 225: 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 45, 75, 225. Common factors: 1, 3, 5, 15, 25, 75. (b) 75 L, the HCF: 150/75 + 225/75 = 2 + 3 = 5 cans. (c) A usable size must be a common factor: 15 L and 25 L work; 30 L is a factor of 150 but not of 225 (225/30 = 7.5), and 50 L is a factor of 150 but not of 225. (d) 15 L: 10 + 15 = 25 cans, 25 x Rs 20 = Rs 500. 25 L: 6 + 9 = 15 cans, 15 x Rs 35 = Rs 525. The 15 L cans are cheaper by Rs 25, even though they need 10 more cans, so fewer cans is not automatically cheaper.
s: (a) both factor lists and the common factors 1, 3, 5, 15, 25, 75
(b) 75 L cans, 5 cans in all
(c) 15 L and 25 L usable; 30 L and 50 L rejected because they do not divide 225
(d) 25 cans costing Rs 500 against 15 cans costing Rs 525
(d) chooses the 15 L cans and notes the fewest cans is not the cheapest

questions.q: Nisha factorises 1050 by dividing by 5, 5, 2, 3 and 7 and reaches 1. Arjun divides 1050 by 2, 3, 5 and 7, reaches the quotient 5, stops there and writes 1050 = 2 x 3 x 5 x 7. Which comment is right?
o: Arjun has dropped the last quotient 5; both should end with 2 x 3 x 5 x 5 x 7
Nisha is wrong, because the division method must begin with the smallest prime 2
Both are right, because a different order of dividing gives a different factorisation
Arjun is right, because each prime can appear only once in a factorisation
questions.a: Arjun has dropped the last quotient 5: 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 is only 210. The division must go on until the quotient is 1, so both get 2 x 3 x 5 x 5 x 7. The order of dividing does not matter, and a prime may repeat.

questions.q: A gardener has 392 saplings, and 392 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 7 x 7. She wants equal rows and checks the possible row sizes using only the prime factorisation. Which row size divides 392 exactly?
questions.a: 56 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 7 is a subpart of 2 x 2 x 2 x 7 x 7, so it divides 392 (392 = 56 x 7). 42 needs a 3, 343 needs three 7s and 16 needs four 2s, which 392 does not have.

questions.q: Rekha looks at 9, 15, 21 and 27 and conjectures: 'Every odd number greater than 1 that is not a prime has 3 in its prime factorisation.' (a) Is her conjecture true? Support your verdict with a counterexample if there is one. (b) Write the prime factorisation of two odd non-primes below 60 that have no 3, and say what one counterexample does to a conjecture.
questions.a: (a) It is false. 25 = 5 x 5 is odd, not a prime and has no 3. (b) For example 35 = 5 x 7 and 49 = 7 x 7 (55 = 5 x 11 also works). A single counterexample is enough to show a conjecture is false, however many examples agree with it.
s: (a) verdict false
(a)/(b) at least one correct counterexample such as 25 = 5 x 5, with a second one such as 35 = 5 x 7 or 49 = 7 x 7
(b) one counterexample is enough to disprove a conjecture

questions.q: (a) Use the division method to write the prime factorisation of 975. (b) Using your answer, decide whether 65 is a factor of 975; if it is, write 975 as 65 times another number.
s: (a) division steps giving 975 = 3 x 5 x 5 x 13
(b) 65 = 5 x 13 is a subpart, so 975 = 65 x 15

questions.q: Kiran conjectures: 'If the prime factorisation of a number contains both 2 and 5, the number ends in 0.' (a) Test the conjecture on 70, 130 and 250 by writing their prime factorisations. (b) Decide whether the conjecture is true for every such number, and explain using subparts.
questions.a: (a) 70 = 2 x 5 x 7, 130 = 2 x 5 x 13, 250 = 2 x 5 x 5 x 5; each has 2 and 5 and each ends in 0. (b) The conjecture is right. If 2 and 5 both appear, then 2 x 5 = 10 is a subpart of the factorisation, so 10 is a factor of the number; a number with 10 as a factor is a multiple of 10 and ends in 0.
s: (a) the three factorisations, each containing 2 and 5, and each number ends in 0
(b) 2 x 5 = 10 is a subpart, so 10 is a factor
(b) verdict: true for every such number, because a multiple of 10 ends in 0

questions.q: Find every number between 200 and 300 whose prime factorisation uses only the primes 2, 3 and 7, each at least once. For one of them, list all its factors that are the product of exactly two of its primes.
questions.a: The numbers must be 42 times a product of 2s, 3s and 7s: 42 x 6 = 252 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 7 and 42 x 7 = 294 = 2 x 3 x 7 x 7 (42 x 4 = 168 is too small and 42 x 8 = 336 too big). For 252 the two-prime subparts are 2 x 2 = 4, 3 x 3 = 9, 2 x 3 = 6, 2 x 7 = 14 and 3 x 7 = 21. (For 294: 6, 14, 21, 49.)
s: finds 252 with factorisation 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 7
finds 294 with factorisation 2 x 3 x 7 x 7, and no other
lists the two-prime subparts of one of them correctly (252: 4, 6, 9, 14, 21 or 294: 6, 14, 21, 49)

questions.q: A school auditorium has 315 chairs to be set out in equal rows. (a) Write 315 as a product of primes by the division method. (b) Using subparts, list every factor of 315, grouping them by how many primes are combined. (c) How many factors are there, and why are they all odd? (d) The hall needs between 10 and 40 chairs in a row. List the possible row sizes and the number of rows for each. (e) Is 27 a possible row size? Decide using the prime factorisation only.
questions.a: (a) 315 / 3 = 105, / 3 = 35, / 5 = 7, / 7 = 1, so 315 = 3 x 3 x 5 x 7. (b) 1; primes 3, 5, 7; two primes 9, 15, 21, 35; three primes 45, 63, 105; all four 315. (c) 12 factors; there is no 2 in the factorisation, so no factor can be even. (d) 15 chairs in 21 rows, 21 chairs in 15 rows, 35 chairs in 9 rows. (e) No: 27 = 3 x 3 x 3 needs three 3s, but 315 has only two.
s: (b) all 12 factors listed by combinations
(c) 12 factors, all odd because there is no 2
(d) row sizes 15, 21, 35 with 21, 15, 9 rows
(e) 27 rejected because it needs three 3s

questions.q: A school library ties 350 Hindi books and 462 English books into bundles, one language per bundle, all bundles of the same size and as few bundles as possible. Given 350 = 2 x 5 x 5 x 7 and 462 = 2 x 3 x 7 x 11, how many books go in each bundle?
questions.a: 14: the common primes are 2 and 7, each appearing at least once in both, so the HCF is 2 x 7 = 14 (25 + 33 = 58 bundles). 7 and 2 leave out a common prime, and 70 wrongly includes 5, which 462 does not have.

questions.q: 600 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 x 5 and 630 = 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7. Consider the following statements about their HCF. Statement 1: It contains exactly one 2. Statement 2: It contains two 5s, because 600 has two 5s. Statement 3: It equals 30. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only: 630 has one 2 and one 5, so the HCF takes the minimum, one 2, one 3 and one 5, giving 30. Statement 2 takes the larger count of 5s, which is the LCM rule, not the HCF rule.

questions.q: (a) Using prime factorisation, find the HCF of 120, 180 and 252. (b) List every number that divides all three exactly.
questions.a: (a) 120 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 5, 180 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5, 252 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 7. Common primes 2 and 3; the fewest 2s is two and the fewest 3s is one, so HCF = 2 x 2 x 3 = 12 (5 and 7 are not common to all three). (b) The common factors are the subparts of 2 x 2 x 3: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
s: (a) three factorisations and HCF 2 x 2 x 3 = 12
(b) common factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12

questions.q: Jaya says: '91 and 143 are both odd and neither ends in 5, so they have no common prime and their HCF is 1.' (a) Write 91 and 143 as products of primes. (b) Is Jaya right? (c) Find the HCF and the number of equal whole-cm pieces of the greatest length that rods of 91 cm and 143 cm can be cut into.
questions.a: (a) 91 = 7 x 13 and 143 = 11 x 13. (b) No. Being odd only rules out 2 and not ending in 5 only rules out 5; they share the prime 13. (c) HCF = 13, so pieces of 13 cm: 91/13 + 143/13 = 7 + 11 = 18 pieces.
s: (b) verdict no, with the reason that odd and not ending in 5 only rule out 2 and 5
(c) HCF 13 and 18 pieces

questions.q: Sunil writes 588 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 x 7 and 840 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 x 7. He says: 'The HCF is 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 = 84. So 12, 14 and 21 are common factors of 588 and 840, but 8 is not.' (a) Check his HCF by taking the smaller count of each common prime. (b) Check each part of his second sentence using the prime factorisations. (c) Give your verdict on Sunil's whole statement.
questions.a: (a) Common primes: 2 (two in 588, three in 840, take two), 3 (one each, take one), 7 (two in 588, one in 840, take one); 5 is not common. HCF = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 = 84. (b) 12 = 2 x 2 x 3, 14 = 2 x 7 and 21 = 3 x 7 are all subparts of 2 x 2 x 3 x 7, so they divide both numbers. 8 = 2 x 2 x 2 needs three 2s, but 588 has only two, so 8 is not a common factor (588/8 = 73.5). (c) Sunil is right on every point.
s: (a) minimum counts taken and HCF 84 confirmed
(b) 12, 14, 21 shown as subparts of the HCF and 8 ruled out because 588 has only two 2s
(c) verdict: the statement is right

questions.q: Kunal writes 336 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 and 504 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 7. He says: 'The HCF is 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 = 168, so 336 and 504 have 168 common factors.' Check both parts of his claim and correct what is wrong.
questions.a: The HCF part is right: minimum counts are three 2s, one 3 and one 7, giving 168. The second part is wrong: the common factors are exactly the factors of the HCF, not 168 of them. Factors of 168: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 14, 21, 24, 28, 42, 56, 84, 168, so there are 16 common factors. Kunal is partly right.
s: confirms HCF 168 with the minimum counts
explains the common factors are the factors of the HCF
counts 16 common factors and gives the verdict partly right

questions.q: A farmers' cooperative in Nagpur has 1260 kg of rice, 1540 kg of wheat and 1890 kg of jowar. Each grain is packed into sacks of the same whole-kg weight, one grain per sack, with nothing left over. (a) Write the three weights as products of primes. (b) Find the heaviest possible sack weight and say how many of each prime it uses and why. (c) How many sacks are needed in all? (d) The loaders say sacks over 50 kg are too heavy to carry. Find the heaviest sack weight they can use, the number of sacks it needs, and say what the cooperative gives up by choosing it.
questions.a: (a) 1260 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7, 1540 = 2 x 2 x 5 x 7 x 11, 1890 = 2 x 3 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7. (b) Common primes 2, 5, 7 (3 is missing from 1540, 11 from the others). Minimum counts: one 2 (1890 has one), one 5, one 7, so HCF = 70 kg. (c) 18 + 22 + 27 = 67 sacks. (d) The usable weights are the common factors, the factors of 70: 1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 14, 35, 70. The largest not above 50 is 35 kg, needing 36 + 44 + 54 = 134 sacks. The cooperative doubles the number of sacks (67 more sacks to buy and fill) in return for loads the workers can lift.
s: (a) three prime factorisations
(b) HCF 70 kg with one 2, one 5, one 7 and reasons
(c) 67 sacks
(d) 35 kg chosen as the largest common factor not above 50
(d) 134 sacks and the trade-off of twice as many sacks stated

questions.q: A milk van visits a village every 4 days and a vegetable van every 10 days. Both came on 1 March. On which date do both vans next come on the same day?
questions.a: 21 March: the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ... and of 10 are 10, 20, ..., so the lowest common multiple is 20 days after 1 March. 3 March uses the HCF 2, 15 March adds 4 + 10, and 10 April uses the product 40.

questions.q: Match each pair in Column I with its LCM in Column II. Column I: 1. 16 and 20  2. 27 and 36  3. 22 and 33  4. 25 and 35. Column II: a. 66  b. 80  c. 108  d. 175.

Pallavi makes a toran from cloth strips 15 cm long and Rekha from strips 25 cm long, strips placed end to end. Both torans must have the same length. (a) By listing multiples, find the shortest length the two torans can have. (b) How many strips does each girl use for that length?
questions.a: (a) Multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, ...; multiples of 25: 25, 50, 75, ...; the lowest common multiple is 75 cm. (b) Pallavi uses 75/15 = 5 strips and Rekha uses 75/25 = 3 strips.
s: (a) both lists of multiples and the shortest length 75 cm
(b) 5 strips and 3 strips

questions.q: Farida writes 84 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 and 90 = 2 x 3 x 3 x 5. She says: 'The LCM is 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 1260, and every common multiple of 84 and 90 must contain at least two 2s and at least two 3s.' Check both parts of her statement and decide whether she is right.
questions.a: She is right on both parts. Taking each prime the maximum number of times: two 2s (from 84), two 3s (from 90), one 5 and one 7 gives 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 1260. A common multiple must contain 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 as a subpart to be a multiple of 84 and 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 to be a multiple of 90, so it needs at least two 2s and at least two 3s.
s: uses the maximum count of each prime
confirms LCM = 1260
explains why every common multiple has two 2s and two 3s, verdict right

questions.q: Leela writes 84 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 and 105 = 3 x 5 x 7. She says: 'The LCM of 84 and 105 is 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 7 = 2940, because I took the 7 from 84 and the 7 from 105.' (a) Show that 2940 is a common multiple of 84 and 105. (b) Find her error and the correct LCM. (c) How many times the correct LCM is her answer?
questions.a: (a) 2940 = 84 x 35 and 2940 = 105 x 28, so it is a common multiple. (b) For the LCM each prime is taken the maximum number of times it occurs in either factorisation, not added from both lists. 7 occurs once in each, so only one 7 is needed: LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 420. Her claim is wrong. (c) 2940 / 420 = 7, the extra 7 she counted twice.
s: (a) 2940 shown to be divisible by both 84 and 105
(b) error named: 7 taken twice instead of the maximum count once; LCM 420, claim wrong
(c) 7 times, the repeated 7

questions.q: Three toy carts have wheels whose rims measure 24 cm, 40 cm and 45 cm around. Each wheel has a paint mark that touches the floor at the start line, and all three carts roll straight ahead side by side. A mark touches the floor again after every full turn. (a) Write 24, 40 and 45 as products of primes. (b) Find the LCM, saying how many times each prime is taken and from which number. (c) After how many cm do all three marks first touch the floor together again, and how many turns has each wheel made by then? (d) In a corridor 36 m long, how many times after the start do all three marks touch the floor together? (e) The 40 cm wheel is replaced by a 48 cm wheel. Find the new distance and the new count for the 36 m corridor.
s: (a) three prime factorisations
(b) LCM 360 with three 2s, two 3s, one 5
(c) 360 cm and 15, 9, 8 turns
(d) 10 times in 3600 cm
(e) new LCM 720 cm and 5 times

questions.q: Consider the following statements. Statement 1: Two co-prime numbers must both be prime. Statement 2: Two consecutive odd numbers, such as 27 and 29, always have HCF 1. Statement 3: Two even numbers can be co-prime. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only. Statement 1 is false: 8 and 9 are co-prime but neither is prime. Statement 2 is true: a common factor of two consecutive odd numbers must divide their difference 2, and both are odd, so it is 1. Statement 3 is false: two even numbers always share the factor 2.

questions.q: True or False: Tripling both numbers of a pair triples their LCM, so the LCM of 30 and 42 is 3 times the LCM of 10 and 14. Check with prime factorisations.
questions.a: True. 10 = 2 x 5 and 14 = 2 x 7 give LCM 2 x 5 x 7 = 70. Tripling puts one extra 3 into each factorisation: 30 = 2 x 3 x 5 and 42 = 2 x 3 x 7, so the LCM is 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 210 = 3 x 70.
s: verdict True
LCM of 10 and 14 is 70 and LCM of 30 and 42 is 210 = 3 x 70, explained by the extra 3 in each factorisation

questions.q: k is a counting number. Ashok must find the LCM of 4k and 12k without choosing a value for k. What is it?
questions.a: 12k: 12k = 3 x 4k, so 12k is a multiple of 4k, and when one number is a multiple of the other the LCM is the larger number. 4k is their HCF, and 48 x k x k is their product.

questions.q: Vani claims: 'If two numbers are co-prime, at least one of them is odd, and their LCM is their product.' Her friend adds: 'So whenever one of two numbers is odd, they are co-prime.' (a) Test Vani's claim on 8 and 15, and on 9 and 16. (b) Explain why Vani's claim is always true. (c) Decide whether her friend's statement is true, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) 8 and 15: HCF 1, one odd (15), LCM 120 = 8 x 15. 9 and 16: HCF 1, one odd (9), LCM 144 = 9 x 16. (b) If both were even, 2 would be a common factor and the HCF could not be 1, so one must be odd. With no common prime, the LCM takes every prime of both numbers, which is their product. Vani is right. (c) The friend is wrong: 9 and 15 are both odd but their HCF is 3, so they are not co-prime (their LCM is 45, not 135).
s: (a) both pairs tested: HCF 1, LCM 120 and 144 equal to the products
(b) both even would share 2; no common prime makes the LCM the product, so Vani is right
(c) counterexample such as 9 and 15 shows the friend is wrong

questions.q: (a) Without multiplying out, find the HCF of 15 x 14 and 15 x 21 using the common multiplier 15. (b) Check your answer by writing both numbers as products of primes. (c) Predict the HCF of 30 x 14 and 30 x 21 and give the reason for your prediction.
questions.a: (a) HCF = 15 x HCF of 14 and 21 = 15 x 7 = 105. (b) 15 x 14 = 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 210 and 15 x 21 = 3 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 315; common subpart 3 x 5 x 7 = 105. (c) 30 x 14 and 30 x 21 are the earlier numbers doubled, so the HCF doubles: 30 x 7 = 210.
s: (b) factorisations of 210 and 315 confirming 105
(c) 210, with the reason that the multiplier is now 30 (both numbers doubled)

questions.q: Bela studies pairs whose LCM is one of the two numbers. (a) Find the LCM and the HCF of 9 and 63, and of 16 and 48. (b) State a general rule for when the LCM of two numbers equals one of them, and write such a pair using a letter. (c) Rafi claims: 'Whenever the LCM of a pair is one of the numbers, the HCF is the other number.' Decide whether he is right and explain. (d) Can two different numbers have an LCM that equals one of them and also equals their product? Find all such pairs or explain why none exist.
questions.a: (a) 9 and 63: LCM 63, HCF 9. 16 and 48: LCM 48, HCF 16. (b) The LCM is one of the numbers exactly when the smaller is a factor of the larger; such a pair is n and kn for counting numbers n and k. (c) Rafi is right: if the numbers are n and kn, then n is a factor of both and no common factor can exceed n, so the HCF is n, while the LCM is kn. (d) If the LCM is kn and also the product n x kn, then n x kn = kn, so n = 1. So the only such pairs are 1 and any other number, such as 1 and 7.
s: (a) LCM 63, HCF 9 and LCM 48, HCF 16
(b) rule: the smaller divides the larger, written as n and kn
(c) verdict right
(c) explanation that n is the largest common factor of n and kn
(d) only pairs containing 1, with the reason

questions.q: Tanvi uses the division method on 252 and 588. She divides both by 2, then 2, then 3, then 7, and her last row is 3 and 7, which have no common prime. What HCF and LCM does she get?
questions.a: HCF 84, LCM 1764: the HCF is the product of the divisors, 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 = 84, and the LCM is 84 x 3 x 7 = 1764. 252 forgets the 7 in the last row, and 148176 is the product 252 x 588, not the LCM.

questions.q: Each row of Column I gives the HCF, the LCM and one of two numbers. Match it with the other number in Column II. Column I: 1. HCF 4, LCM 120, one number 24  2. HCF 7, LCM 210, one number 35  3. HCF 12, LCM 144, one number 48  4. HCF 1, LCM 77, one number 7. Column II: a. 11  b. 20  c. 36  d. 42.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-c, 4-a, using other number = HCF x LCM / given number: 4 x 120 / 24 = 20, 7 x 210 / 35 = 42, 12 x 144 / 48 = 36, 1 x 77 / 7 = 11.

questions.q: (a) Find the HCF and the LCM of 132 and 198 by the division method, dividing both numbers first by 11 and then by 6. (b) Check that HCF x LCM equals 132 x 198.
questions.a: (a) 132/11 = 12 and 198/11 = 18; 12/6 = 2 and 18/6 = 3; the last row 2, 3 has no common factor. HCF = 11 x 6 = 66 and LCM = 66 x 2 x 3 = 396. (b) 66 x 396 = 26136 and 132 x 198 = 26136, so they are equal.
s: (a) table with rows 12, 18 and 2, 3, giving HCF 66 and LCM 396
(b) both products equal 26136

questions.q: Two numbers have HCF 12 and LCM 72. Pinky says: 'The numbers must be 12 and 72.' (a) Check that 12 and 72 do have HCF 12 and LCM 72. (b) Use HCF x LCM = product to find their product, then decide whether Pinky's word 'must' is right by looking for another pair.
questions.a: (a) 72 = 12 x 6, so the HCF of 12 and 72 is 12 and the LCM is 72. (b) The product of the two numbers is 12 x 72 = 864. Both numbers are multiples of 12, so they are 12a and 12b with a x b = 6 and a, b sharing no factor (the same as a division table by 12 whose last row has no common factor and multiplies to 6): a, b = 1, 6 gives 12 and 72; a, b = 2, 3 gives 24 and 36. Check: 24 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3, 36 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3, HCF 12, LCM 72. So her pair works, but the claim that the numbers must be 12 and 72 is wrong.
s: (a) 12 and 72 checked
(b) product 864 and the second pair 24 and 36 found and checked (accepts the 12a, 12b form or a division-table argument with a co-prime last row)
(b) verdict: the claim is wrong, because 12 and 72 are not the only pair

questions.q: Three pupils start the division table for 252 and 396 differently. Anu divides both by 4 and then by 9. Babu divides by 6 and then by 6 again. Charu divides by the primes 2, 2, 3 and 3. (a) Write each pupil's rows down to the last row. (b) Find the HCF and the LCM from each table. (c) Explain why all three tables must give the same HCF.
questions.a: (a) Anu: 63, 99 then 7, 11. Babu: 42, 66 then 7, 11. Charu: 126, 198; 63, 99; 21, 33; 7, 11. Every table ends with 7 and 11, which have no common factor. (b) HCF = 4 x 9 = 6 x 6 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36 in each; LCM = 36 x 7 x 11 = 2772 in each. (c) Each pupil has removed all of the common part 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36 before reaching 7 and 11; only the grouping of the divisors differs, so the product of the divisors, the HCF, is the same.
s: (a) all three tables ending in 7, 11
(b) HCF 36 and LCM 2772 from each table
(c) the divisors in each table multiply to the same common part 36

questions.q: (a) For each pair, find the HCF, the LCM and the product: 36 and 54; 35 and 48; 40 and 100. (b) Explain why the product of two numbers is always a common multiple of them, and so why the LCM can never be greater than the product. For which of the three pairs is the LCM equal to the product, and why? (c) Two numbers have LCM 504 and product 3024. Find their HCF. (d) Find every such pair of numbers. (e) Which of these pairs have both numbers between 20 and 200?
questions.a: (a) 36, 54: HCF 18, LCM 108, product 1944. 35, 48: HCF 1, LCM 1680, product 1680. 40, 100: HCF 20, LCM 200, product 4000. (b) a x b is b times a and a times b, so it is a common multiple; the LCM is the lowest common multiple, so it is at most the product. For 35 and 48 they are equal, because the HCF is 1 (co-prime). (c) HCF = 3024/504 = 6. (d) Both numbers are 6 times numbers p and q with p x q = 84 and no common factor (or: a division table by 6 whose last row has no common factor and multiplies to 84). (1, 84), (3, 28), (4, 21), (7, 12) give 6 and 504, 18 and 168, 24 and 126, 42 and 72. (e) 24 and 126, and 42 and 72.
s: (a) HCF, LCM and product for all three pairs
(b) product is a common multiple, so LCM is at most the product; equal for 35 and 48 as they are co-prime
(c) HCF 6
(d) the four pairs found (accepts the 6p, 6q form or a division table by 6 with a co-prime last row multiplying to 84)

questions.q: A fruit seller finds that her mangoes can be shared equally among 4, among 6 or among 9 children with none left over. She has more than 50 and fewer than 100 mangoes. How many does she have?
questions.a: 72: the number must be a common multiple of 4, 6 and 9, that is, a multiple of their LCM 36; between 50 and 100 that is 72. 36 is too few, 54 cannot be shared among 4, and 216 is the product, far above 100.

questions.q: Ravi's stride is 60 cm and Sita's is 75 cm. Starting together from the same line, each puts a chalk mark at the end of every stride along a 12 m corridor. How many times after the start line do their marks fall on the same spot?
questions.a: 4: marks meet every LCM(60, 75) = 300 cm, so at 3 m, 6 m, 9 m and 12 m. 5 counts the start line too, 80 divides 1200 by the HCF 15, and 36 = 20 + 16 counts all the strides.

questions.q: True or False: The smallest number of beads that can be threaded equally on strings of 4 or on strings of 6 with none left, but leaves 3 beads over when threaded on strings of 5, is 48. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The number must be a common multiple of 4 and 6, that is a multiple of their LCM 12. Testing in order: 12, 24, 36 leave remainders 2, 4, 1 on division by 5, and 48 = 5 x 9 + 3 leaves 3. So 48 is the smallest.
s: verdict True
multiples of the LCM 12 tested in order, showing 12, 24, 36 fail and 48 leaves 3

questions.q: On a circular track, Arun takes 6 minutes per lap and Bindu 10 minutes per lap. They start together from the start line. The coach says: 'They will next be together at the start line after 30 minutes, and by then Arun will have run 2 more laps than Bindu.' Check both parts and give your verdict.
questions.a: Arun is at the start after 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, ... minutes and Bindu after 10, 20, 30, ... minutes, so the first common time is the LCM, 30 minutes. In 30 minutes Arun runs 30/6 = 5 laps and Bindu 30/10 = 3 laps, a difference of 2. The coach is right on both parts.
s: LCM of 6 and 10 found as 30 minutes
5 laps and 3 laps worked out
verdict: both parts right

questions.q: For a school fair, a ground 72 m by 120 m is to be marked into equal square plots of whole-metre side, with no land left over. Along the boundary of the whole ground, starting at the gate corner, a red flag is put every 6 m, a yellow flag every 8 m and a blue flag every 16 m, going right round. (a) Find the largest possible plot side and the number of plots it gives. (b) How far from the gate, along the boundary, is the first point after the gate that carries all three flags? (c) The boundary is 384 m long. How many points on it, including the gate, carry all three flags? (d) The organisers need at least 30 plots. Find the largest plot side that gives at least 30 plots and the number of plots, and explain why the plan in (a) does not meet the need.
questions.a: (a) Common factors of 72 and 120: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24; HCF 24 m, giving 3 x 5 = 15 plots. (b) LCM of 6 = 2 x 3, 8 = 2 x 2 x 2 and 16 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 = 48 m. (c) 384/48 = 8, and 384 is a multiple of 6, 8 and 16, so the pattern closes at the gate: the points 0, 48, ..., 336 m, that is 8 points. (d) 24 m gives only 15 plots, too few. The side must be a common factor; the next one, 12 m, gives 6 x 10 = 60 plots, at least 30. So 12 m, with 60 plots.
s: (a) HCF 24 m and 15 plots
(b) LCM 48 m
(c) 8 points including the gate
(d) 15 plots rejected as fewer than 30
(d) 12 m chosen as the next common factor, giving 60 plots

questions.q: In a game of 'Fire in the Mountain', children must form groups of the number called out, and those left without a group are out. When 4 was called, no one got out; when 6 was called, no one got out; when 10 was called, some children got out. Which of 24, 36, 48, 60 and 72 could be the number of children? Explain.
questions.a: No one out for 4 and for 6 means the number is a common multiple of 4 and 6, that is, a multiple of their LCM 12. All five numbers are multiples of 12. Some children out for 10 means the number is not a multiple of 10, which rules out 60. So the number could be 24, 36, 48 or 72.
s: the number is a multiple of the LCM 12
60 ruled out because it is a multiple of 10
answer 24, 36, 48 or 72
